iterations.theme: Scientific foundation of nutrition in cycling and carbohydrate intake: professionals versus recreational riders

sections.subtitle: Introduction to the podcast: Who is Luka Batur and why is nutrition the key to success?
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur in the studio explains his education and experience in sports nutrition.
sections.content:
In the sixteenth episode of the biciklizam.net podcast, host Josip hosted Master of Nutrition Luka Batur, author of a nutrition guide for cyclists and an active triathlete. The occasion for the conversation was a series of new scientific papers that analyze in detail nutrition in professional cycling in the period from 2016 to 2025.

At the very beginning, Josip asked the guest to present his professional and sporting credibility. Luka Batur pointed out that he graduated from the Prehrambeno-biotehnološki fakultet of the Sveučilište u Zagrebu, where he gained a deep understanding of chemistry and human metabolism, which he considers a key difference compared to self-taught advisors. After completing university, he worked at KBC Zagreb as a dietitian, and today he collaborates with numerous professional athletes, amateurs, but also people with clinical diagnoses.

Along with theoretical and clinical knowledge, Batur has been active in triathlon since 2017, which allows him to hone scientific postulates through personal experience in the field. He emphasized that he continuously follows global trends, attends leading sports congresses like the one in Manchester, and adapts the acquired knowledge to what is truly feasible for athletes and recreational riders in practice.

sections.subtitle: Marginal gains and nutritional secrets in the modern peloton
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur gestures while speaking about tiny details and advantages of professional cycling teams.
sections.content:
The conversation then turned to the specifics of cycling as a sport that was historically burdened by the stigma of doping, but in the modern era the focus has radically shifted toward the concept of so-called *marginal gains* — tiny details that added together bring victory.

Josip and Luka Batur agreed that today's professionals ride technically very similar, top-tier bicycles and conduct equally grueling training processes, which is why nutrition is becoming one of the main areas where an advantage over the competition is created. Batur pointed out that top teams engage scientists who are at the same time skilled practitioners in the field.

Nevertheless, many nutritional strategies, muscle biopsy testing, and specific protocols are kept as a strict professional secret. Research in teams is conducted for years before its results are publicly published at all, because no leading team wants to yield its discoveries to competitors.

sections.subtitle: The scientific elite behind the new UCI papers on cyclist nutrition
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains the role of leading world scientists in creating new guidelines.
sections.content:
Speaking about the new series of papers that attracted great attention from the cycling public, Luka Batur emphasized that the very cream of sports nutrition stands behind them. Among the key authors are names such as Ascker Jeukendrup, who worked for years with team Jumbo-Visma, and then moved to Bora-Hansgrohe, and James Morton, known for work with team Sky/Ineos and leading football clubs, as well as Australian scientist Louise Burke.

Batur pointed out that Ascker Jeukendrup had even earlier revolutionized sports nutrition with the discovery of optimal ratios of glucose and fructose (such as ratios of 2:1 or 1:0.8), which enabled the absorption of more than the standard 60 grams of carbohydrates per hour. The guest also described the atmosphere from professional conferences where these scientists without hesitation publicly enter into heated debates — such as discussions on RED-S syndrome (relative energy deficiency in sport) — but despite disagreements continue to collaborate on new research.

This new series of papers, as Batur explained, represents a comprehensive review (*comprehensive review*) of current findings, enriched with notes directly from the field (*personal observations* of nutritionists at Grand Tour races), and was published in open access (*open access*), which makes it an exceptionally valuable source of information.

sections.subtitle: From caloric needs at a Grand Tour to mobile kitchens
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur with notes in hand lists the topics covered by the new scientific papers.
sections.content:
Analyzing the content of the published paper, Josip and Luka Batur reflected on the fact that today's cycling races are significantly faster and more demanding than ever before, which leads to enormous caloric expenditure. The paper elaborates in detail how energy needs drastically change depending on the stage profile — from flat sections where intake is lower, to difficult mountain stages that require maximum energy availability.

Batur emphasized that the paper covers the entire annual periodization. An average professional competes for about 80 days a year, while spending the rest of the time in training and recovery, where proper nutrient timing is crucial for preserving health and avoiding injuries. Special chapters are dedicated to dietary supplements, distinguishing useful supplements from ineffective or dangerous ones, as well as specifics of sports food like gels and bars.

As a particularly interesting segment, Batur singled out the paper titled *From Plate to Performance*, which is dedicated to the functioning of mobile kitchens at races. In it, the collaboration between nutritionists and professional chefs whose task is to translate dry numbers and caloric calculations into tasty, digestible, and appealing meals for exhausted riders is described in detail.

sections.subtitle: The myth of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour: Should recreational riders copy professionals?
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains the difference in carbohydrate intake between professionals and amateurs.
sections.content:
One of the most important topics of the conversation was carbohydrate intake on the bike and the increasingly present trend among recreational riders who try to reach the famous number of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour, inspired by elite professionals. Luka Batur emphasized that carbohydrates are primarily „rocket fuel” and that intake must be strictly dictated by the intensity and duration of the ride, and not by a mere desire to break records in sugar intake.

Batur explained that professionals on mountain stages ride for hours at an exceptionally high percentage of their VO2 max, expending huge glycogen stores, while recreational riders on group rides or in zone 2 expend incomparably less energy:
- **Demanding races and high intensities:** Justify an intake of 90 to 120 g/h (with prior training of the digestive system).
- **Recreational rides and amateurs:** For 80 to 90 percent of cyclists, an intake of 30 to 60 g/h is completely sufficient to maintain a stable energy level.
- **Low-intensity rides (brevets, coffee rides):** It is enough to eat by feel (one bar or banana per hour along with liquid), without the need for complicated weighing and forcing gels.

Batur concluded that exaggerating intake during lower-intensity training brings recreational riders more harm than benefit — from digestive issues and nausea to unnecessary calorie intake — because higher intake on paper does not automatically mean crossing the finish line faster if the body cannot utilize that energy intake.

iterations.theme: Physiology of digestion, injury prevention, and practical examples of nutrition at races

sections.subtitle: Gels versus bars: Why avoid fats, fiber, and protein under exertion
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur gestures with his hands explaining the composition of bars and why to avoid protein on the bike
sections.content:
Considering practical choices of nutrition during a ride, Josip and Luka Batur open the eternal dilemma of cyclists: gels or bars? Batur points out that the choice primarily depends on the intensity of the ride and the dynamics of the terrain. When riding at a high pace in the peloton, at a heart rate of 170 beats per minute, it is extremely dangerous and technically difficult to remove hands from the handlebars to chew solid food, which is why liquids and gels become an absolute priority. On the other hand, bars and solid food are reserved for calmer sections of the route, but should by no means be consumed immediately before or at the very beginning of demanding climbs.

When solid food is chosen, science and practice dictate one key rule: the bar must contain as little fat, fiber, and protein as possible. Even though it is a solid form, it should essentially be almost pure carbohydrate. The reason lies in the physiology of digestion – fats, proteins, and dietary fiber significantly slow gastric emptying and the transit of nutrients through the intestines into the bloodstream, while under exertion the primary goal is to deliver glucose to the muscles as quickly as possible.

Batur especially emphasizes the absurdity of consuming protein bars during a ride. Proteins do not serve as an efficient energy source on the bike, and the fear of losing muscle mass during several hours of exertion is completely unfounded because overall daily protein intake is crucial for muscle preservation. Also, Batur warns of the common amateur mistake of delaying meals on the bike. As a workout or race progresses, the body redirects blood from the digestive system to the working muscles of the extremities, which drastically reduces intestinal motility and digestive efficiency. For that reason, it is necessary to start carbohydrate intake within the first fifteen to twenty minutes of exertion, while the digestive system is still optimally perfused and capable of absorbing nutrients without stress and stomach issues.

sections.subtitle: How science discovered absorption limits: The role of SGLT1 and GLUT5 transporters
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains the action of intestinal glucose and fructose transporters
sections.content:
The question of how scientists arrived at the famous number of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour leads directly into laboratory research and the study of intestinal physiology. Luka Batur explains that scientists used stable isotopes (such as carbon C13) with which they labeled carbohydrate solutions, and then through indirect calorimetry and analysis of exhaled carbon dioxide precisely measured how much of the ingested substance was actually oxidized in the muscles.

To determine where the bottleneck in the human body is located, researchers gave athletes infusions of glucose directly into the bloodstream. The results showed that muscle tissue is capable of utilizing almost the entire amount of glucose delivered by the blood, which indisputably proved that the limit does not lie in the muscles, but in the digestive tract, that is, at the level of the intestinal barrier.

Further research illuminated the transport mechanism through the intestinal wall. Glucose uses specific carriers known as SGLT1 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 1), whose capacity is saturated at approximately 60 grams per hour. However, the turning point came with the realization that fructose enters cells via a completely independent transporter system (GLUT5). Combining glucose and fructose made it possible to use both entry channels simultaneously, thereby raising the total capacity of carbohydrate delivery into the bloodstream to 90 and up to 120 grams per hour without causing severe gastrointestinal distress.

sections.subtitle: Homemade alternatives to gels: Plain sugar, salt, and honey
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur answers viewer questions about homemade concoctions and gel replacements
sections.content:
To a viewer's question about whether expensive commercial gels and drinks can be replaced with plain table sugar and a pinch of salt, Luka Batur answers affirmatively, recalling how he himself during his student days, for financial reasons, bought pure glucose or maltodextrin in pharmacies and drugstores and prepared mixtures himself. Plain consumable white sugar (sucrose) consists of glucose and fructose in a 50:50 ratio, but Batur warns that sucrose in higher concentrations can cause digestive issues in more sensitive individuals, which is why he still gives preference to maltodextrin or pure glucose.

When it comes to honey as a natural substitute, Batur expresses skepticism primarily due to practical and logistical reasons. Besides honey being a rather expensive source for regular consumption in training, its viscosity makes packaging, carrying, and squeezing on the bike under high exertion extremely difficult.

As an accessible and functional alternative for low- and moderate-intensity workouts, Batur often recommends plain gummy candies. The fundamental conclusion comes down to intensity and goals: as long as the athlete sticks to an intake of up to 60 grams of carbohydrates per hour, precise sugar ratios, branded forms, and expensive factory additives are not crucial. Commercial gels show their true advantage only at competitions, where their practical packaging and optimized osmolarity enable lightning-fast energy intake without chewing and burdening the stomach.

sections.subtitle: Injury prevention through nutrition: RED-S syndrome and the dangers of caloric deficit
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur in a serious tone explains the dangers of RED-S syndrome and calorie deficit
sections.content:
Although injury prevention in sports is customarily tied to stretching, warm-up, and the gym, Luka Batur emphasizes that nutrition plays a crucial, often neglected role in preserving the integrity of the musculoskeletal system. The key problem is represented by the relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S) syndrome, which occurs when athletes train for weeks or months with insufficient energy intake relative to expenditure, often motivated by a desire to reduce body weight.

Batur warns of the severe consequences of a long-term deficit, which he regularly encounters in practice, particularly among young female athletes. When the body recognizes a lack of energy for basic survival, it shuts down functions that are not essential, leading to the loss of the menstrual cycle (amenorrhea), a drop in estrogen levels, and disrupted bone density. As a result, young girls of barely twenty years old can develop osteopenia or osteoporosis, making their bones brittle and prone to stress fractures and more severe fractures during falls. Similar consequences are also recorded in men through a drastic drop in testosterone.

Scientific papers clearly point out that supplements like calcium or vitamin D have a secondary effect if the basic caloric need is not met. Batur emphasizes that amateurs often make the mistake of eating a quality meal immediately after training, and then starve for the rest of the day or uncontrollably eat inadequate food, remaining in a massive deficit. When voluminous workouts of four or five hours are conducted, daily needs can reach up to 10 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body mass, which demands a strategically planned and abundant intake in order to prevent chronic fatigue, an immunity drop, and severe injuries.

sections.subtitle: A practical example: How Luka fueled before, during, and after a granfondo
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur with a smile describes meals and the amount of coffee he drank before the race
sections.content:
To translate theory into reality, Luka Batur described in detail his own nutritional protocol for participating in a granfondo that he finished in 2 hours and 42 minutes. Preparation began the day before, on Saturday, when he applied a carbohydrate loading protocol. To avoid overloading the digestive tract with an excessively large volume of solid food, he reduced fats and fiber to a minimum, and focused on easily digestible sources: he ate a 400-gram package of apple strudel, a generous portion of Čokolino, pasta with a light sauce, and replaced part of his daily fluids with Cedevita and juices.

On race day, which started at 10:45, breakfast was again based on Čokolino mixed with skim milk along with the addition of cake. Immediately before the race he drank nearly half a liter of coffee and half an hour before the start ate a handful of gummy candies along with a Red Bull energy drink for caffeine stimulation. On the bike itself he carried two bidons with isotonic drink totaling 120 grams of carbohydrates and six gels, five of which he consumed during the ride (about 100 grams). Intake began already after the first 15-20 minutes of the ride, and with aid stations he took in a total of about 200 grams of carbohydrates in 2 hours and 42 minutes of racing.

After crossing the finish line, Batur immediately approached glycogen store restoration. He consumed the bolognese served, and at home ate prepared forest fruit as a rich source of antioxidants and carbohydrates, continuing with a lunch rich in potatoes, meat, and birthday desserts. He pointed out that intense exertion empties stores to such an extent that it has been recorded in papers that even an intake of 13 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of mass in 24 hours sometimes fails to completely restore glycogen, which is why after races one must not hesitate with the intake of quality food.

sections.subtitle: How to preserve muscle mass and properly dose proteins
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur analyzes protein intake and strength training for cyclists
sections.content:
Responding to a viewer inquiry about how cyclists and participants in multi-day bikepacking tours can preserve muscle mass without accumulating adipose tissue, Luka Batur dispels common misconceptions. First of all, he emphasizes that nutrition alone cannot build or preserve muscle if adequate mechanical stimulus is lacking – for muscle maintenance, specific strength training, namely resistance work in the gym, is necessary.

Regarding protein intake, Batur reiterates that taking protein during the ride itself has no effect on performance or on preventing catabolism during those few hours. Only total daily protein intake distributed across meals before and after the activity is crucial. According to valid scientific evidence, an amount of 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body mass daily is completely sufficient for maintenance, and even for muscle hypertrophy in endurance athletes, which is very easily achieved with a standard diet rich in meat, fish, eggs, or dairy products.

On extended bikepacking adventures of several weeks, it is completely natural for an athlete to lose part of upper body strength if not visiting the gym, but for shorter trips of five to seven days there is no reason to panic. Batur concludes that there is no need to do strength exercises at rest stops in the middle of a ride; rather, it is sufficient to ensure a stable protein intake through breakfast and dinner, while the focus on the bike itself must remain on the primary fuel – carbohydrates.

iterations.theme: Nutrition on long distances, supplementation in cycling, and final conclusions

sections.subtitle: Nutrition on brevets and misconceptions about taking magnesium
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur gestures explaining why bacon and eggs are not a good food choice on long rides.
sections.content:
In the continuation of the conversation, host Josip poses a question from viewer Damir Vibre regarding nutrition on long-distance rides like brevets. Damir states that during rides he often consumes sandwiches with eggs and bacon, water, and is interested in the optimal timing of taking magnesium. Master of Nutrition Luka Batur emphasizes that the combination of eggs and bacon represents a poor choice for cycling because fats and proteins drastically slow gastric emptying and make energy absorption difficult. Considering that the body already has sufficient fat stores at its disposal, it is unnecessary to burden the digestive system with them at the expense of much-needed carbohydrates.

Batur advises milder options such as lean cold cuts or light spreads so that the ride passes without gastrointestinal issues and heaviness in the stomach. He especially addressed the myth of taking magnesium before and during physical activity. Magnesium loss through sweating is negligible, and recommendations for its intake during riding actually do not exist in modern sports science. Moreover, most commercial forms such as magnesium oxide or carbonate have extremely poor absorption and often cause a laxative effect. Batur recommends taking higher-quality forms, such as magnesium bisglycinate, exclusively in the evening hours for relaxation and better sleep.

sections.subtitle: Balancing nutrition with obligations and resolving evening sweet cravings
sections.screenshot_description: Close-up shot of Luka Batur as he describes typical nutritional mistakes of recreational riders after a long workout.
sections.content:
To viewer Dejan's question about how to balance nutrition with an accelerated daily routine and curb strong cravings for sweets, Luka Batur points out that an uncontrollable need for chocolate is almost always a direct consequence of a chronic carbohydrate deficit. In practice, a common scenario is that a cyclist drinks a beer after an exhausting Sunday ride, and eats a large amount of meat with minimal potatoes or pasta for lunch. By evening, the body recognizes a lack of glycogen, which regularly results in bingeing on cream spreads and chocolates.

As a solution, Batur proposes a planned increase in carbohydrate intake on days with intense workouts. He advises regular consumption of fruit, freshly squeezed juices, rice, pasta, and potatoes without unfounded fear of weight gain:

- Increase carbohydrate side dishes in main meals instead of overdoing meat.
- Include fresh fruit and squeezed juices in snacks as a practical source of energy.
- Ensure sufficient glycogen intake throughout the day to prevent nighttime hunger attacks.

Batur emphasizes that food should not be a reward that an athlete must 'earn', but a strategic fuel that enables faster recovery and a higher-quality training process.

sections.subtitle: Combining different carbohydrate sources and testing tolerance
sections.screenshot_description: Josip asks viewer questions from paper while Luka listens and prepares an answer about energy sources.
sections.content:
A viewer from Serbia asked a question regarding an eight-hour ride and the dilemma of whether it is better to use only two to three carbohydrate sources or a wider spectrum of foods. Batur explains that during exceptionally long exertions, combining different formats (liquids, gels, energy bars, and gummy candies) is not only desirable, but also recommendable. Long-term consumption of exclusively one type of flavor or texture often leads to so-called sensory saturation and nausea.

For recreational riders and brevet participants, the choice is significantly more flexible than in competitive races, but the key to success lies in testing during workouts. Batur cites the example of a client who meticulously kept a spreadsheet rating sports gels by stomach tolerance, texture, and sweetness before choosing a winning combination. The conclusion is that every cyclist must try products from different manufacturers on easier rides in order to determine what their digestive tract tolerates best under exertion.

sections.subtitle: Lamb, veal, or fish in cyclist nutrition
sections.screenshot_description: Relaxed atmosphere in the studio as the host and guest laughingly comment on gastronomic questions.
sections.content:
In a humorous tone, Josip read a question from a viewer interested in whether spit-roasted lamb or veal under the peka is a better choice for cyclists. Luka Batur laughingly admitted that he would disappoint lovers of traditional cuisine, noting that his father is a professional fisherman and that he himself holds a commercial fishing certificate, which is why he always gives preference to fish.

Nevertheless, from a nutritional standpoint both meats are acceptable if consumed in moderate quantities outside of competition phases and heavy workouts themselves. Batur notes that his partner and triathlete Marija Lukina does not eat white chicken meat at all, which shows that top athletes can successfully function with different protein sources, provided that overall energy intake is balanced.

sections.subtitle: Beetroot juice and nitrates: Increasing efficiency and economy
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur uses his hands to demonstrate the difference between work economy and oxygen consumption in athletes.
sections.content:
Moving on to the topic of specific dietary supplements, Batur analyzed in detail the role of beetroot juice and inorganic nitrates. The mechanism of action of nitrates is based on vasodilation and improving mitochondrial economy, which enables the athlete to produce the same work with less oxygen consumption. This raises overall efficiency on the bike.

An interesting scientific finding points out that beetroot juice has a significantly more pronounced effect on amateurs and recreational riders than on top athletes with VO2 max values above 65 ml/kg/min. It is presumed that professionals, through years of training process, have already reached the physiological maximum of adaptations. The protocol that Batur recommends and applies himself ahead of races like the Half Ironman includes an intake of half a liter of beetroot juice daily (or concentrated extracts) across three to seven days before the main competition.

sections.subtitle: Supplement overview: Caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, and baking soda
sections.screenshot_description: The guest in the studio lists supplements from the list of scientifically proven substances in cycling.
sections.content:
Batur reflected in detail on supplements that possess a solid scientific basis in cycling. Caffeine was highlighted as one of the most effective ergogenic aids because it is proven to reduce the perception of fatigue in doses of 3 to 6 mg per kilogram of body mass. However, he warns that caffeine should not be taken in the late afternoon hours so as not to impair sleep quality and subsequent recovery. He also refutes the myth of the need for winter 'weaning' off coffee, stating that research does not show a significant loss of sensitivity among regular consumers.

Analyzing other dietary supplements, Batur singles out specific groups of riders:

- **Creatine**: Useful for sprinters, disciplines like cyclocross and mountain biking with explosive accelerations, and accelerates glycogen synthesis. On the other hand, cyclists focused on long climbs often avoid it due to a possible body weight increase of 0.5 to 1 kg.
- **Beta-alanine**: Effectively buffers hydrogen ions (H+) during submaximal and maximal intervals. It is ideal for athletes who conduct structured interval training.
- **Baking soda (sodium bicarbonate)**: A premier extracellular buffer, but requires extreme caution because in standard forms it causes severe stomach and intestinal distress, unless specialized hydrogel systems are used.

sections.subtitle: UCI paper conclusion: Recovery, beer and pizza after a ride, and sign-off
sections.screenshot_description: Closing shot of host Josip and guest Luka Batur as they say goodbye to the podcast viewers.
sections.content:
In the closing part of the conversation, Batur summarizes the messages of the extensive review paper on cyclist nutrition. The key conclusion is that amateurs should not blindly copy extreme intakes of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour if their riding intensity does not require it. A much more important factor is the overall quality and quantity of food during the rest of the day. Also, he warns of the danger of excessive intake of high doses of synthetic antioxidants (such as vitamins C and E in tablets) during the preparation period because they can blunt the body's natural training adaptations.

Touching upon the myth of pizza and beer as recovery aids, Luka clearly points out that alcohol dehydrates the body and directly inhibits muscle glycogen resynthesis. Although one beer after a recreational ride will not cause harm, athletes aiming for top results must, immediately after exertion, prioritize rehydration, liquid carbohydrates, and proteins. Host Josip concludes the episode with an invitation to viewers to support the idea of regular nutrition videos with Luka Batur on the channel and download his nutrition guide for cyclists.
